A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'), and the other options are plainly absurd ('rice needs no water'). A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

rejected.title: The economic value of water
card: Water has economic value because people use it to earn a living and to run towns. Farms, factories and homes all depend on it.
Irrigation means supplying water to crops by channels, pipes or sprinklers. It lets farmers grow crops where rain alone is not enough.
The Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area in New South Wales grows rice with irrigation water. The Mekong Delta in Vietnam also grows rice with irrigation.
Towns grow where water is reliable, because workers, shops and services need it. If water supply drops, farm output and local jobs can be affected.
rejected.remember: Water has economic value because it helps people earn money and keeps farms and towns running.

a.q: Why does a river's water have economic value for a farming district?
opts: It lets farmers grow crops that they can sell
It makes the district look more attractive
It is a place with cultural meaning for locals
It stops any need for farmers to plan ahead
a.why: Irrigation water helps farmers grow crops to sell, and this earns money for the district. Beauty and cultural meaning are real values, but they are not the economic value described here.
a.clue: Think about how water helps people earn a living.

b.q: A dry spell cuts the irrigation water for a rice-growing town in the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area. What is the most likely effect on the town?
opts: Less rice is grown, so local farm work may fall
More rice is grown, because farmers work harder
Nothing changes, because rice needs no water
The town gains jobs, because rice is cheaper
b.why: Rice grown with irrigation needs a reliable water supply. With less water, less rice is grown and there may be less farm work. Working harder cannot make up for less water.
b.clue: What happens to crops when irrigation water falls?

flags: Question b, wording: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'), and the other options are plainly absurd ('rice needs no water'). A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

a.q: What gives a river's water economic value to a farming district?
opts: It lets farmers grow crops that they can sell
It makes the district look more attractive
It holds cultural meaning for people there
It cools the district on hot summer days
a.why: Irrigation water helps farmers grow crops to sell, and this earns money for the district. Beauty and cultural meaning are real values, but they are not the economic value described here.
a.clue: Think about how water helps people earn a living.

b.q: In a dry year, less irrigation water is sent to rice farms in the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area. What is the most likely effect on the nearby towns?
opts: Smaller rice harvests mean less farm work in town
Bigger rice harvests, as dry weather suits rice
More farm jobs, as extra workers carry water
No effect, since most of the rice is sold overseas
b.why: The rice there is grown with irrigation, so less water means less rice. Smaller harvests mean less farm work, which affects jobs in nearby towns. Selling rice overseas does not protect the towns, because the money and jobs still depend on how much rice is grown.
b.clue: Follow the water to the crop, then to the workers.
